planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring after frost danger passes; Golden Hills is a female cultivar released by UC Davis and needs a male pollinator such as Randy or Peters blooming at the same time within wind-pollination range.

directions: Golden Hills is a female pistachio cultivar developed by the University of California, Davis, and released in the early 2000s to give California growers an alternative to the industry-standard Kerman. It leafs out and blooms roughly one to two weeks earlier than Kerman, which lets it pair with earlier-flowering male pollinators and helps spread orchard harvest timing, and it is noted for bearing more consistently from year to year with less pronounced alternate bearing. Like all pistachio, it needs the same demanding regime of 700-1000 winter chill hours and long, hot, dry summers to fill and split its shells, so it performs poorly in humid climates even where winters are cold enough. Grow it in deep, well-drained, alkaline soil, and expect several years of establishment before the tree reaches significant nut production.
sources: University of California, Davis — Pistachio Variety Development
University of California Cooperative Extension — Pistachio Production Manual

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in full sun on well-drained, even poor sandy soil; Hergo is a German female cultivar and needs a male pollinator such as Pollmix within about 50-100 feet for fruit set.

directions: Hergo is a German-bred female sea buckthorn cultivar prized for producing some of the largest individual berries of any named selection, borne in tight orange clusters along the previous year's wood, which makes it a favorite for growers pressing juice or oil at a small commercial scale. It ripens in mid-season, generally a bit ahead of the largest Russian selections, and shares the thorny, silvery-leaved, nitrogen-fixing growth habit typical of the species. As a dioecious shrub it sets little or no fruit without a nearby male sea buckthorn in bloom at the same time. Because the tart berries cling firmly to the stem, most growers harvest by cutting whole fruiting branches and stripping or freezing them rather than picking individual berries by hand.
sources: Julius Kühn Institute — German Sea Buckthorn Breeding Program

planting.note: Set out a bare-root or container-grown Andrews shrub in early spring into moist, well-drained soil; a second seedling or cultivar nearby improves cross-pollination and fruit set.

directions: Andrews is a named selection of American highbush cranberry chosen by northern breeders for producing larger, less bitter fruit than typical wild seedlings, making the tart red berries more pleasant for fresh sauces and jelly without as much of the musky flavor common to the species. Like the straight species it is a true Viburnum rather than a cranberry, blooming with flat white lacecap clusters in late spring before setting heavy fruit clusters that ripen in fall and persist on the shrub well into winter as valuable cold-season wildlife food. It is exceptionally cold-hardy, tolerating northern Great Plains and prairie winters that few fruiting shrubs survive, and grows best in consistently moist, well-drained soil. Prune out the oldest canes at the base every few years to keep the multi-stemmed shrub vigorous and productive.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or bare-root nursery stock in spring into well-drained, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; plant two or more seedlings for cross-pollination, since Hansen's selections are largely self-unfruitful.

directions: Hansen's Bush Cherry is the classic named strain of western sandcherry selected and distributed by South Dakota State plant breeder N.E. Hansen in the early 1900s specifically for fruit quality, chosen out of wild seedling populations for larger, sweeter, purple-black cherries than the straight species typically bears. It remains one of the most reliable fruiting shrubs for the Northern Great Plains and prairie provinces, tolerating extreme winter cold, drought, and alkaline soils that eliminate most other stone fruits. Plants bloom with abundant white flowers in early spring and ripen fruit in mid- to late summer, useful fresh, dried, or cooked into jam, syrup, and wine, though flavor and astringency vary somewhat from seedling to seedling since it is propagated as an open-pollinated strain rather than a single clone. Prune out the oldest stems at ground level every few years to renew fruiting wood on this low, spreading shrub.
